nodes.name: U.S. Federal Government
nodes.note: Root of the map.

profile.overview: The United States Federal Government is the top-level public authority, not a single research-funding agency or a direct application channel for university spinouts. Federal support for early-stage companies is delivered through departments and agencies, each with its own programmes, solicitations, and award decisions. The Small Business Administration coordinates the government-wide SBIR/STTR framework, while participating agencies set their own technical priorities and run their competitions.
profile.venture_arm: unknown
profile.annual_budget_note: No single venture-arm budget; funding is appropriated and administered by individual agencies and programmes.
profile.application_timeline: There is no government-wide application cycle. Deadlines depend on the specific agency and programme; SBIR/STTR solicitations are issued by participating agencies.
profile.eligibility: There is no root-level applicant eligibility or application process. Eligibility is set by each funding programme; SBIR/STTR generally requires a qualifying U.S. small business.
profile.relationship_note: This is the root of the map, not a funding arm to approach. HHS, Defense, DOE, NSF, NASA, Commerce, DHS, USDA, DOT, EPA, Education, Treasury, and the other mapped entities administer their own programmes and make their own awards. SBA coordinates the SBIR/STTR framework and provides government-wide policy and information, but applicants submit to participating agencies, which set topics, solicitations, and award budgets. Grants.gov is an application-discovery and submission portal for many federal grants, not a funder or a substitute for an agency programme office.
profile.uncertainty_note: The root has no consolidated venture funding mechanism or budget. Programme details and current opportunities must be verified with the relevant agency.

nodes.name: HHS
nodes.full_name: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
nodes.note: Largest funder of biomedical research in the world; parent of NIH, BARDA, ARPA-H, FDA, CDC.

profile.overview: The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is the cabinet department responsible for federal health and human-services activities. It is the parent of agencies and offices including NIH, ASPR, ARPA-H, FDA, CDC, and AHRQ, which set their own research and commercialization priorities. HHS does not operate one department-wide venture fund; the main route for eligible companies is through SBIR/STTR solicitations issued by participating HHS components. A company should identify the relevant component and solicitation rather than approach HHS as a single grantmaker.
profile.venture_arm: HHS SBIR/STTR opportunities issued by participating HHS components; applications are made to the component and specific solicitation, not to a centralized HHS venture fund.
profile.annual_budget_note: No consolidated HHS-wide SBIR/STTR budget figure is provided here. Participating components have separate solicitations and budgets.
profile.application_timeline: There is no single HHS-wide application calendar. Deadlines and submission routes depend on the participating component and its specific SBIR/STTR solicitation; check the relevant component's current notice before planning a submission.
profile.eligibility: For SBIR/STTR, applicants generally must meet federal small-business eligibility rules, including U.S. ownership and operation and applicable size, control, and research-performance requirements. STTR requires a formal research-institution partner. Component-specific solicitation rules apply.

profile.relationship_note: HHS is the department-level umbrella, not a unified funding desk: its operating components issue their own SBIR/STTR solicitations and make awards. NIH is the major biomedical SBIR/STTR route within HHS, while CDC, FDA, AHRQ, and ASPR-related opportunities address their own missions; ARPA-H uses its own program mechanisms as well. Do not assume an NIH solicitation, budget, or award ceiling applies to another HHS component. SBA, a sibling department, sets government-wide SBIR/STTR policy and runs key program infrastructure, while HHS components define the topics and award opportunities.

nodes.name: NIH

profile.overview: The National Institutes of Health is an agency within HHS and the largest federal funder of biomedical research. Its principal route for early-stage companies is the NIH SBIR/STTR program, a shared mechanism through which participating NIH institutes and centers fund small businesses. Those institutes and centers set scientific priorities and make funding decisions within the shared framework; NIH SEED provides program guidance and commercialization support rather than a separate major award pool. NIH also funds research through mechanisms outside SBIR/STTR, but those are not generally direct company venture funding.

The relevant institute or center sets the scientific fit, uses its own program priorities and available allocation, and is generally the key decision-making home for an application; applicants should identify that fit before choosing a topic or submitting. NIH SEED supports navigation, education, and commercialization but is not a separate substitute funding pool. The listed NIH institutes and centers are therefore program-level routes into the shared mechanism, rather than independent siblings with wholly separate SBIR systems. nodes.note: The single largest source of non-dilutive funding for health startups. Institutes fund against it from their own budgets.

profile.overview: NIH SBIR/STTR is NIH’s agency-wide small-business funding mechanism, not a standalone institute or a single centrally funded award programme. NIH institutes and centers issue opportunities and make awards from their own budgets, choosing topics and priorities within the SBIR/STTR framework. It funds research and development by eligible U.S. small businesses, from early feasibility work through later-stage development. NIH SEED provides programme coordination and small-business support, but applicants generally apply to a specific NIH institute or center opportunity.

profile.overview: NIH SEED (Small business Education and Entrepreneurial Development) is NIH’s cross-agency entry point for small businesses and entrepreneurs working with NIH-supported research. It provides commercialization education and navigation, rather than serving as an institute-level grantmaker or investment fund. Its support includes I-Corps at NIH and Concept to Clinic: Commercializing Innovation (C3i), which help teams develop commercial readiness. NIH Institutes and Centers remain the route for applying for NIH SBIR/STTR funding.
profile.venture_arm: NIH SEED entrepreneurial assistance programs, including I-Corps at NIH and Concept to Clinic (C3i); these provide non-financial commercialization support, not investment or an award.
profile.annual_budget_note: No separate annual budget for SEED's entrepreneurial assistance programs confirmed.
profile.application_timeline: Programs are cohort-based and announce their own application windows; timing and availability vary. Check the SEED site for current I-Corps at NIH and C3i opportunities.
profile.eligibility: Eligibility is program-specific. These programs generally serve teams commercializing NIH-supported biomedical technologies, often including NIH SBIR/STTR applicants or awardees. Check the current program announcement for required award status, team composition, and other criteria.

profile.relationship_note: SEED is a cross-NIH support and navigation function, not a replacement for NIH SBIR/STTR or the Institutes and Centers that issue those awards. A company seeking non-dilutive funding applies through the relevant NIH SBIR/STTR opportunity and selects an appropriate Institute or Center; SEED's programs can complement that funding with commercialization training. NIH I-Corps is nested within SEED on this map. C3i is translational commercialization support, not a separate source of grant capital. Unlike NCATS, SEED is not principally a translational grantmaking center.

profile.overview: NIH Innovation Corps (NIH I-Corps) is an NIH SEED program that teaches biomedical small businesses how to test the commercial assumptions behind an NIH-funded innovation. It is a cohort-based customer-discovery programme, rather than a general research grant or an equity investor. It is intended for teams with an NIH SBIR/STTR Phase I award and can help them turn technical progress into evidence about customers, markets, and routes to adoption. For a university spinout, it is a commercialization support step after an NIH award, not a substitute for obtaining one.

profile.overview: The National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS) is an NIH center focused on improving the process of moving discoveries toward clinical use. For companies, its most direct funding route is NCATS participation in NIH-wide SBIR/STTR solicitations, where applicants must match their proposed work to an NCATS topic and active funding announcement. NCATS also offers translational development support, including BrIDGs, which provides drug-development services rather than a cash award. Its Clinical and Translational Science Awards primarily support institutions and research infrastructure, not startup financing.

Its NCI SBIR Development Center helps small businesses pursue NCI-funded research and development, principally through SBIR and STTR awards and some topic-specific contracts. A university spinout can apply directly if it meets federal small-business eligibility rules; the work must fit NCI's cancer-related priorities. NCI's funding is part of the broader NIH small-business system, but NCI sets its own program priorities and awards its own share of funding.

For companies and university spinouts, its main direct funding route is NHLBI participation in the NIH SBIR/STTR programs. NHLBI also supports translation through resources such as SMARTT, which provides development services rather than a separate investment or grant mechanism. Its SBIR/STTR priorities and portfolio decisions are specific to NHLBI’s mission, while application rules and much of the process are shared across NIH.

A company can seek NCCIH support through NIH-wide mechanisms, including SBIR/STTR, when its proposed work fits NCCIH’s priorities and a relevant funding opportunity. NCCIH does not have a separate venture fund or investment vehicle.

nodes.name: ASPR

nodes.note: HHS's preparedness arm; parent of BARDA.

profile.overview: The Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR) is the HHS agency responsible for preparing for and responding to public health emergencies. Its main route for supporting companies developing medical countermeasures is BARDA, which sits inside ASPR; BARDA’s DRIVe initiative focuses on earlier-stage innovations. ASPR is therefore not a single, agency-wide seed fund: opportunities, award terms, and technical priorities depend on the BARDA program or solicitation. A university spinout should look for a specific BARDA or DRIVe opportunity rather than apply to ASPR generally.

It is a plausible non-dilutive partner for a spinout with promising data and a product relevant to public-health preparedness, but it is not a general-purpose startup grantmaker. Companies engage through BARDA solicitations and acquisition mechanisms, including contracts and other transactions. Its nested initiatives have different roles: DRIVe is oriented toward earlier innovation, while Project BioShield supports procurement of qualifying countermeasures.

It supports companies through the DRIVe Accelerator Network and BARDA’s EZ-BAA, a competitive contracting route for promising technologies. The accelerator network provides business and technical support; it is not itself the same thing as a funding award. For a university spinout, DRIVe is a potential source of non-dilutive development funding and commercialization support, rather than an equity investor.

Companies, including startups, can compete for project awards, but ARPA-H is not an equity investor and does not offer one standard award size or application cycle. Its Open BAA and mission-office solicitations are the main routes to propose work.

profile.overview: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is an HHS agency whose main role is regulating medical products, foods, and other FDA-regulated products—not financing companies. Its relevant early-stage support includes the FDA Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program, clinical-trial grants for orphan products, grants to pediatric device consortia, and CDRH’s non-financial Total Product Life Cycle Advisory Program (TAP). These mechanisms can help a company fund product development or navigate regulatory and commercialization questions, but they are separate programmes with different applicants and eligibility rules.

profile.relationship_note: FDA is an HHS sibling of NIH, ASPR, and ARPA-H, but it is primarily a regulator rather than a broad health-research funder. Its SBIR programme is FDA’s own agency mechanism, not an NIH award; use the FDA solicitation and topics rather than assuming NIH deadlines or priorities. EERE also identifies topics for DOE SBIR/STTR solicitations, but those small-business awards use DOE's centrally administered SBIR/STTR process rather than a separate EERE application system. Its priorities and opportunities are organized around energy technology programmes, so applicants should follow the specific solicitation rather than assume one EERE-wide application cycle.

nodes.name: OCED

profile.overview: The Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (OCED) is a DOE office that funds large-scale demonstrations intended to move clean-energy technologies toward commercial deployment. Its programs are generally project-based competitions, often involving consortia, rather than small-business awards or equity investments. A company may participate as a project lead or partner when a specific funding opportunity allows it, but the fit depends on the opportunity’s scale, cost share, and team requirements. OCED is most relevant to university spinouts with a technology ready to demonstrate at meaningful scale.
profile.venture_arm: OCED competitive project funding, primarily grants and cooperative agreements for clean-energy demonstrations. This is not a dedicated startup or equity-investment program; a company would apply to a specific funding opportunity, often as part of a larger project team.
profile.annual_budget_note: No stable annual venture-arm budget. OCED funding is appropriated and allocated to specific multiyear programs and project competitions; check the relevant notice for current funding and award limits.

EERE also funds technology development and deployment, so applicants should compare each office’s specific notice rather than assume a single hand-off. DOE SBIR/STTR is a separate small-business mechanism: an SBIR award does not confer eligibility or priority in OCED competitions, and OCED projects are commonly larger and require partners and cost share. The Loan Programs Office is a potential complementary source of debt financing for later commercial deployment, not a substitute for OCED demonstration grants. The Office of Technology Transitions supports commercialization and technology transfer but is not OCED’s project-funding mechanism.
profile.uncertainty_note: The office’s role and broad funding model are stable, but award sizes, cost-share requirements, eligibility, and application steps differ substantially by program and funding announcement. profile.overview: The DOE Loan Programs Office (LPO) provides federal debt financing—direct loans and loan guarantees—for eligible U.S. energy and advanced-vehicle projects. It sits within DOE and is not a grant programme or equity investor: applicants need a project with a credible path to repayment, and financing is generally aimed at commercial deployment rather than basic research. A university spinout may be relevant when it can sponsor or join a financeable project, but LPO is usually not the first non-dilutive funding step for a lab-stage company. Financing terms and eligibility depend on the specific statutory programme.

For companies, its main commercialization route is America’s Seed Fund, NSF’s SBIR/STTR program, which supports technical feasibility and product development rather than taking equity. The Directorate for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (TIP) houses this commercialization activity and sets its strategic direction. NSF’s remit is broad and generally non-clinical; medical research and product development may fit better at HHS or another mission-focused agency.

It sits inside NSF, rather than operating as a separate agency or a single grant programme. A spinout seeking direct federal startup funding will usually apply through NSF Seed Fund (SBIR/STTR), while other TIP programmes support different steps in translation.

The main team-level mechanism provides a modest award alongside an intensive training cohort; it is not a seed investment in a company. Its practical value is helping a research team decide what to commercialize and how to approach the next funding step.

profile.relationship_note: SSBCI is Treasury's principal route to startup financing, but it is an intermediary funding structure: Treasury funds state, territorial, and Tribal programs, and those programs or their partners make financing available to businesses. This differs from siblings such as HHS, DOE, and NSF, which run agency SBIR/STTR solicitations that companies apply to directly. It also differs from SBA's direct federal small-business support mechanisms; SSBCI is separately administered by Treasury through participating jurisdictions. A university spinout should start with its state's SSBCI program rather than Treasury's headquarters, and should not assume that an SSBCI award is a standard federal grant or that program terms are uniform across states.

profile.overview: The State Small Business Credit Initiative (SSBCI) is a U.S. Treasury program that provides capital to states, territories, and Tribal governments to operate small-business financing programs. It is not a federal grant or investment that a startup applies for directly: a company seeks financing through a participating state or Tribal program. Those programs can include venture capital as well as loan participation, guarantees, collateral support, and other credit support. For a university spinout, the relevant route depends on the state where it operates and the SSBCI-backed program available there.
profile.venture_arm: State- and Tribal-administered SSBCI-backed financing programs, including venture capital programs where offered. Companies apply to the relevant local program or fund, not to Treasury.
profile.annual_budget_note: No single annual venture-arm budget or standard company check size: allocations and deployment terms vary by participating jurisdiction and program. Treasury describes SSBCI as a $10 billion multi-year program, not an annual startup investment budget.
focus_areas: State-administered venture capital for eligible small businesses
Technical assistance connected to accessing SSBCI capital
profile.application_timeline: There is no single federal application cycle for companies. Availability, deadlines, and intake processes are set by each participating state, territory, or Tribal government and its program or fund.
profile.eligibility: A company does not apply to Treasury for SSBCI financing. It applies to a participating state, territory, or Tribal program and must meet that program's rules, including applicable small-business and use-of-funds requirements. Eligibility, geography, stage, and investment terms vary by program; confirm them with the local administrator before applying.
materials_required: Program-specific application and company information
Business plan and use-of-funds description, if required by the local program
Financial, ownership, and eligibility information required by the local program
For venture investments, any diligence materials requested by the participating fund
profile.relationship_note: SSBCI sits within Treasury, but Treasury allocates funds to participating jurisdictions rather than selecting or financing individual startups. This makes it a different route from federal SBIR/STTR: SSBCI is state- or Tribal-administered capital, while SBIR/STTR are agency research awards. A university spinout should identify the SSBCI-backed fund or credit program in its relevant jurisdiction and build a relationship there; the existence of an SSBCI allocation does not mean that jurisdiction offers venture equity or that a particular company is eligible.
profile.uncertainty_note: The program's overall structure is stable, but available products, company eligibility, check sizes, application timing, and local contacts vary by jurisdiction. Verify these with the specific SSBCI-backed state, territory, or Tribal program.
